newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: VAL aims for dominance in metallurgical plant.
newsitem.headline: VAL aims for dominance in metallurgical plant.

text.p: Austria's Voest-Alpine Industrieanlagenbau GmbH said on Wednesday it aimed to become the world's leading supplier of metallurgical plant by strengthening its rolling mill manufacturing businesss.
"Steelmaking and casting plants are our core competence. But we also want to push our rolling mill techniques", VAI's chief executive, Horst Wiesinger, told Reuters in an interview.
"Around 50 percent of all investment in the industry goes into rolling mills and strip finishing bands", he added.
A strip finishing band is a device which puts a coating, such as paint or galvanised zinc, on rolled strip steel.
VAI, a unit of technology group VA Technologie, recently won a contract to build a new strip coating line for British Steel at its Llanwern works in south Wales.
Rolling mill orders reached 4.5 billion schillings in 1996 after just 700 million two years ago, Wiesinger noted. The firm provisionally reported record sales and order intake in 1996.
New orders jumped from 9.5 to 15.5 billion schillings, boosted by a six billion schilling order from Saudi Arabia. Sales were up 65 percent to 9.2 billion schillings, he said.
Wiesinger forecast growth in both North and South America, as well as in the Far East, and stagnation in European markets.
"We want to become a major player in the United States and raise our market share from 10 to 20 percent", Wiesinger said.
VAI aims to attract annual new order intake of two billion schillings in North America in the next few years, he said.
COREX, a new technology which will in future replace conventional blast furnaces, is expected to account for the bulk of additional orders.
"The new compact steel plant of the future will be smaller, tailored to the needs of our clients", he said.
Wiesinger said VAI was working to ensure lasting technological leadership and efficiency, which he said was crucial because of enormous price pressures.
"Steel will still play a big role in the future", he said. By the year 2005, worldwide production would expand to 813 tonnes from 750, Wiesinger forecast.
There was also room to improve the quality of steel. "The development of material has not been completed," he said.

One of Wiesinger's goals was to set up an institute subsidised by the state to work on material research in cooperation with firms like VA Stahl AG, high-grade steel maker Boehler Uddeholm and refractories producer Veitscher which would be "natural partners".
